big_idea: Most communication breakdowns come from unconscious psychological, biological, and cultural patterns, early conditioning, defensive reactions, ego states, rather than a simple lack of vocabulary, and shifting from control talk to mindful dialogue is what actually fixes them.

tool.label: Connect, control, dialogue talk
tool.text: Kehoe frames most conversations as falling into three modes: connect talk, small talk and rapport-building; control talk, commands, blame, and escalation; and dialogue talk, mindful, mutual, collaborative exchange. Recognizing which mode you're in is the first step to shifting toward dialogue.
tool.note: Runs through all 24 lectures and is paired with other frameworks he cites, including transactional analysis and the ladder of inference.

ideas.title: Talk shapes self
ideas.text: Self-concept and communication habits are formed young, through childhood conversations with caregivers, and often operate unconsciously in adulthood.

ideas.title: Schema-based perception
ideas.text: We don't hear what's said so much as we interpret it through mental templates built from past experience, a major source of miscommunication.

ideas.title: Control talk escalates
ideas.text: Light and heavy control patterns, commands, accusations, blame, are common default reactions under stress and tend to trigger defensiveness.

ideas.title: Active listening is underused
ideas.text: Genuinely listening, not just waiting to respond, is one of the most neglected and most powerful communication skills.

ideas.title: Gender and cultural patterns
ideas.text: Discusses report talk versus rapport talk gender differences and broader cultural influences on how people communicate.

ideas.title: Dialogue as practice
ideas.text: Mindful, compassionate confrontation and structured dialogue are taught as learnable techniques for turning conflict-prone conversations into collaborative ones.

try_it: For one day, notice every time you slip into control talk and try re-phrasing it as a question instead.
Practice one I-message this week instead of a you accusation in a tense conversation.
Before responding in your next disagreement, pause and ask yourself which assumption you're filtering the other person's words through.
Try one deliberate active-listening exercise: reflect back what you heard before adding your own point.
best_for: People who want the psychological why behind miscommunication
Listeners who prefer structured academic-style teaching
less_useful: Readers wanting quick tactical scripts over theory
Those who already know transactional analysis or similar frameworks

related.why: A structured language practice for moving out of control talk into dialogue
A modern take on matching your communication mode to the conversation at hand
